metadata.title: The CRA Ladder.
metadata.subtitle: Concrete–Representational–Abstract, One Lesson
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: what does differentiating fraction addition across three levels actually look like when it's one lesson, not three? The CRA ladder runs Concrete, Representational, and Abstract as three entry points into the SAME target — 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6 — with the design trade-off being that the tool has to watch the climb, not just the arrival. Lands the carry-out: Claude builds one shared target with three rungs, tested by whether every rung reaches the abstract result without skipping a step.

beats.narration_text: Instinct says three levels means three lessons. That's not what CRA is doing. It's one lesson with three rungs — concrete, representational, abstract — and the design question is whether every rung actually reaches the same answer.

beats.narration_text: One third plus one half. That's the problem. CRA gives it three ways in, all landing at the same place. Concrete — fraction circles: push a one-third piece and a one-half piece together and watch five sixths appear. The answer is physical before it's symbolic. Representational — a tape diagram split into thirds and halves. You find the shared unit, sixths, before you touch the arithmetic. Abstract — the equation itself: one third plus one half equals two sixths plus three sixths equals five sixths. A student below grade level enters on the circles, at grade level on the tape, above on the equation. Three doors, one room. That's the design move — not three lessons, one target with three ways to reach it.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — three rungs, one ladder, 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6

beats.narration_text: The design move worth naming is the arrows between the rungs, not the rungs themselves. Three journeys run in parallel, all aimed at the same abstract destination. A student who reaches five sixths on the circles is ready for the tape diagram. One who can draw the diagram is ready for the equation. The rungs aren't three tracks — they're one staircase with three places to start climbing. What CRA optimizes for is upward mobility across representations; what it costs you is an evaluator that watches for the climb, not just the arrival.

Here's the catch: the expertise-reversal effect. The concrete support that helps a beginner — the physical fraction pieces in hand — becomes noise for a student who already holds the representational picture in mind. Same aid, opposite direction: for the novice it's a bridge; for the expert it's clutter that costs attention. That's why the CRA ladder isn't a fixed setting attached to a student. It's a path, and the rung that helped yesterday can hurt today. Judge the choice against that fact — a ladder that never lets you climb off it stops being a ladder.

production_viz.label: THE RUNG THAT HELPED YESTERDAY
production_viz.caption: the rung that helped yesterday is noise today

beats.narration_text: Scaffolding, when it works, honors a three-part contract. Contingency — the support matches where the learner is right now, not where the syllabus says they should be. Fading — the support is withdrawn as skill grows, on purpose. Transfer — the learner ends up doing it alone. Skip fading and the support that once matched five sixths on the circles just stays there, forever. The way you find out whether a rung was scaffolding or a permanent prop is to pull it out and see if the learning still holds. That test is what separates a ladder from a prosthesis.

beats.narration_text: Claude doesn't build three separate lessons — it builds one shared target with three rungs to reach it, and the test is whether every rung gets there without skipping a step.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I have a sixth grade lesson on solving one-step equations. Design the full CRA progression — a concrete task with physical or visual manipulatives, a representational task with a diagram, and an abstract task with the algebra itself — as three entry points into one lesson, each rung built so a student who succeeds on it is ready for the next. Then tell me what fading looks like for this lesson: how do I know which rung to remove, and when. Go deeper: once the progression exists, ask what evidence would tell you a student is ready to climb from one rung to the next — and what the lesson looks like if that evidence never comes.
